items.body:
## Summary

Exposes each FPGA's HBM thermal status registers (`hbm_thermal_north` / `hbm_thermal_south`) as on-demand FUSE stats and exported Prometheus gauges:

```
/rinzler/stats/hbm_thermal/<bdf>/N_temprd   degrees Celsius, north HBM stack
/rinzler/stats/hbm_thermal/<bdf>/N_temp     3-bit refresh-rate indicator (3 = normal)
/rinzler/stats/hbm_thermal/<bdf>/N_cattrip  catastrophic-temperature trip flag
/rinzler/stats/hbm_thermal/<bdf>/S_*        same for the south HBM stack
/rinzler/stats/hbm_thermal/<bdf>/idx        casual: rinzler's internal device index
```

**Location example** (Rinzler TP4):
```
wmiller@andoria-15:attn_tron$ ls -l /scratch/wmiller/hbm-thermal-poke/stats/rinzler/stats/hbm_thermal/
total 0
dr-xr-xr-x 15 wmiller wmiller 0 Sep  4 17:54 01:00.0
dr-xr-xr-x 15 wmiller wmiller 0 Sep  4 17:54 21:00.0
dr-xr-xr-x 15 wmiller wmiller 0 Sep  4 17:54 41:00.0
dr-xr-xr-x 15 wmiller wmiller 0 Sep  4 17:54 61:00.0
```

**Example output**:
```
wmiller@andoria-15:attn_tron$ pho tron stats read --path /scratch/wmiller/hbm-thermal-poke/stats/rinzler/stats/hbm_thermal
(root)
                                                                           
 fpga_bdf  N_cattrip  N_temp  N_temprd  S_cattrip  S_temp  S_temprd  idx   
 01:00.0   0          3       68        0          3       67        3     
 21:00.0   0          3       65        0          3       65        1     
 41:00.0   0          3       67        0          3       67        2     
 61:00.0   0          3       59        0          3       59        0     
```

## Design

- **Keyed by PCI address.** rinzler's `PosDevice::idx` (libpci scan order), the BMC/`pho bw cards` slot number, and ascending PCI order all number the cards differently (on andoria-15, rinzler idx 0 is BDF `61:00.0`, which is `pho` card 7). The dimension value is the BDF and the column/Prometheus label is `fpga_bdf`, so a reading is unambiguous in every tool. The `idx` sidecar leaf (unexported) decodes rinzler log lines that print only `dev N`.
- **Lazy registration.** Called from `get_devices()` once workers are ready; a no-op when FUSE stats are not mounted, so it works for both rinzler (static files before `start()`) and runtron (dynamic files picked up on rescan).
- **tronstats convention.** `tronstats_marker` gains an optional `name` so a `.descriptor.yaml` can relabel a dimension column; the subtree's marker sets `category: thermal` (a category documented in the Tronstats Structure spec) and `name: fpga_bdf`. Metric descriptors follow the existing dynamic-family pattern (`register_tronstats_hbm_thermal_metrics`).

## Test plan

- `t_tronstats_convention` extended: thermal dynamic family (leaf creation, registration, `.{metric}.yaml` shape, expected-set), `"thermal"` added to the allowed categories, and `assert_canonical` now also checks the marker's `name`. Runs in the existing CI suite. 1200 assertions / 30 cases pass.
- Verified live on andoria-15: FUSE leaves and `.descriptor.yaml` present, `pho tron stats read` renders the table above, values track across restarts, `idx` matches rinzler's own `dev N (BDF)` log lines.

items.title: Attention: skip ranges without software work

labels.name: Performance
labels.description: Makes things go faster

items.body:
Skip per-query scans of attention pages already covered by hardware offload. Preserve software tails and partial-page visibility, and fix Pending readiness checks for pages shared by multiple writers.

**Large reductions in Ready worker time during both prompt and generation; no material overall model speedup demonstrated.** GPT-OSS-120B TP4, one user at 32K context, hardware attention enabled:

| Phase | Reduction in summed Ready worker time |
| --- | ---: |
| Prompt / prefill | **76.7%** (2.64 → 0.614 s) |
| Generation / decode | **37.3%** (29.6 → 18.6 ms) |

Within Ready sections with no estimated software work, the reductions are **99% for prompt** and **47.9% for generation**. These are overlapping worker spans, averaged across three matched trace pairs. Repeated untraced model checks at 2K and 32K, including four users at 2K, show equivalent throughput and latency (less than 1% difference).

**Potential gain:** removing these scans frees workers and may improve model performance when CPU attention becomes a bottleneck. That larger benefit has not been measured.

**Pending sections:** the increase reproduces at **2.14% more prefill worker time** across three fresh pairs (+3.05%, +2.03%, +1.35%), versus **5.2%** in the original single pair. Generation Pending averages **2.65% more worker time**, driven by one pair (+6.72%; the other two are within 1%). These are summed worker times; no corresponding full-model latency or throughput regression has been measured. Pending generally contains new pages requiring computation. The readiness fix waits for every writer of a readable physical page and deduplicates checks for consecutive tokens sharing that page.

Validation:

- `t_llama_unit`: 128,487 assertions / 30 cases; `t_ranged_mask`: 262 assertions / 25 cases. Both passed at 1, 2 and 4 slices; benchmark metadata is refreshed.
- Restoring only the old producer-token visibility predicate makes both shared-page readiness cases fail; the other 29 cases pass.
- Pinned clang-format-19, applicable Lefthook checks and `make build-test` passed.
- CI: [host tests](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/actions/runs/34655835716/job/103452391973) **92 passed, 0 skipped, 0 failed**, including the proxy suite; [FPGA tests](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/actions/runs/34655835716/job/103452392013) **53 passed, 0 skipped, 0 failed**. All 19 checks in that CI run passed.

Performance checks used clean, frozen Nix `cross-avx512` RelWithDebInfo builds and the same GPT-OSS-120B TP4 plugin, weights and prompt tokens. Both ran through public Distributed Dice wrappers on **andoria-cf8c, NUMA0**, with NUMA1 idle for the primary comparisons. Hardware attention was enabled at engagement 127; sliding-window layers retain software attention. No live-token or per-user prompt-chunk override was set.

One-user sweeps used three isolated iterations per version, the same 32K→2K runtime order, 32,769 / 2,049 actual input tokens, 128 generated tokens. The four-user CI-style control used 2,048 input tokens per user, 514 generated tokens. Multi-user samples average the four correlated request measurements within each fresh batch.

Reversing run order and extending the four-user control to ten isolated iterations did not reproduce a consistent generation slowdown. Raw model measurements are preserved in the recorded artifacts.

Three fresh matched trace pairs use GPT-OSS-120B TP4, one user, 32,769 input tokens and 128 generated tokens, with alternating base/head order. With `--trace-passes 249-264` and categories `-*,+model,+scheduler,+hwattention`, all six included captures have **zero loss and zero incomplete slices**: eight 128-query prefill forwards, the final one-query prefill forward, and seven decode forwards. One incomplete capture was excluded and replaced.

| Traced work | Mean summed worker time (ms), base → head | Change (lower is better) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Prefill Ready, all | 2,640 → 614 | **-76.7%** |
| Prefill Ready, zero estimated software work (subset of above) | 1,860 → 17.8 | **-99%** |
| Prefill Pending | 721 → 737 | **+2.14%** |
| Generation Ready | 29.6 → 18.6 | **-37.3%** |
| Generation Ready, zero estimated software work (subset of above) | 23.6 → 12.3 | **-47.9%** |
| Generation Pending | 4.51 → 4.63 | **+2.65%** |

The worker-time savings do not establish an overall model speedup; the separate untraced runs supply the model results.

items.title: fix K/V DMA geometry and eligibility bounds for models with fewer than 8 KV heads
items.body:
## Why

Running ingested qwen3-30b-a3b with hardware attention failed on the very first forward pass with
`Encountered NaN s_star`. It happened at tp2 and tp4, from a 16-token prompt upward. Every other hardware
attention model we run has 8 KV heads; qwen3-30b has 4, and it was the first model to exercise that
difference.

The cause was in how the K cache is written to the FPGA. The hardware reserves a fixed slot for each token:
room for 8 KV heads of 128 elements, regardless of what the model actually has. The code that writes K
assumed the slot was only as wide as the model's KV head count. With 8 heads the two agree. With 4 heads,
the second, third and fourth tokens in every block of four were written to the wrong place, and the FPGA
read K values that had never been written. V was already laid out for 8 heads, which is why the failure
showed up in the softmax denominator rather than in the attention output.

Fixing that and testing it at 4 heads surfaced a few related problems, all fixed here as separate commits:

- The V write path had its own geometry bug. The "readback fence" (the word the host waits on to know a
  DMA has landed) was placed based on the transfer length instead of the row size, so at 4 heads it pointed
  past the bytes being written. Production does not use the fence, but the tests do.
- Several helpers silently clamped an unsupported KV-head count instead of rejecting it.
- A model with 32 or more query heads per KV head would pass the hardware-eligibility check and then abort
  at runtime, because a 5-bit command field cannot hold that ratio.
- The debugging code that reads K back from HBM used the wrong geometry too, and nothing in the tree
  compiled it, so it had rotted unnoticed.

This is unrelated to the `NaN v_star` failure seen in the field on 8-head models.

## What changed

**K cache DMA.** Positions within a block are now stepped by the hardware's fixed slot size. The transfer
still carries only the heads the model has. This is the fix for the qwen3 failure and it changes nothing for
8-head models.

**V cache DMA.** The transfer length and the readback fence are now both derived from the block's row
layout, so the fence always sits inside the bytes the DMA writes. Production behavior is unchanged.

**Rejecting unsupported shapes.** Every K and V transfer helper now asserts that the KV-head count is
between 1 and 8 instead of clamping it. The eligibility check that decides whether a model may use hardware
attention now also requires `n_heads / n_kv_heads <= 31`, which is what the 5-bit `gqa` field can hold.
A shape past that limit takes software attention instead of aborting on the first hardware command. The
runtime assertions and the worker reference the same constant, so the limit is defined once.

**K cache readback (debug only).** The reader now inverts the exact layout the writer produces, so a dump
of a model with 64-wide heads is no longer scrambled. The dump header is compiled by one test target so
future drift is caught at build time.

**Documentation.** The hardware attention doc now says K is written as one contiguous descriptor per token
(splitting by head across FPGAs is planned, not implemented) and has a corrected V layout table. Two helpers
carry doc comments answering questions raised in review: why one keeps a `head_size` parameter production
never varies, and that the other is test-only.

## How it was tested

**Batch test at 4 and 8 KV heads.** `t_hwattention_batch` now runs its whole battery at both head counts.
To make a wrong K write visible, the test first fills every K slot with a poison value through the 8-head
path, then writes the real K through the path under test. K is filled so that each query has a known
correct maximum score; if any slot still holds poison, that maximum comes back wrong. The unused V rows are
poisoned the same way and the attention output is checked against the source values. K and V are loaded
using the same descriptor path production uses, so the test covers the code that actually runs in serving,
not only the blocking helper.

Each fix was proven red/green on hardware by temporarily restoring the old behavior:
- Old K stride: the 8-head case passes, the 4-head case fails every query with the poison value.
- Old K descriptor path in the test: the previous test still passed with a broken production stride (that
  was the gap); the new test fails 4768 checks, every one reading the poison score.
- Old K readback: the round-trip test fails at the third element of a 64-wide head.

items.title: Prevent DMA descriptor-ring laps from corrupting attention KV
items.body:
## Summary

- prevent the load-weight DMA descriptor producer from lapping the FPGA consumer
- make completion wrap accounting race-free without blocking completion pollers behind a backpressured producer
- expose descriptor-backpressure frequency and latency through FUSE stats
- add attention `s_star`/`v_star` NaN tripwires
- **removes the original WCLS WCMD deferral, which turned out to be a red-herring**

## Root cause

Deep dual-Rinzler MMLU serving creates shared-prefix KV backfill bursts large enough to overrun the 32,768-entry load-weight DMA descriptor ring. The producer could lap and overwrite outstanding descriptors even though completion wrap inference assumed that could never happen. Software then reported unfinished DMA as complete, released/reused GOF staging, and let HW attention consume incomplete or corrupt K data, producing NaN `s_star`/`v_star` values that subsequently poisoned WO and later layers.

## Fix

`xfer_blocks()` and `xfer_n_blocks()` now reserve capacity for payload and crossed link descriptors before writing the ring. Reservation preserves one empty physical slot, applies backpressure until the consumer advances, and uses a progress-based timeout so slow draining is not mistaken for a wedge.

Producer wrap and submitted tail are published as one atomic position, and consumer-head sampling is serialized under a dedicated mutex. This prevents torn producer state and out-of-order consumer samples from advancing completion accounting by a lap. FUSE counters report episode count, total wait time, and maximum wait time.

## Verification

In addition to the typical 'make test-host' and such:

The full CI-shaped Qwen3-4B TP4 MMLU campaign ran 10 times with fresh dual Rinzlers at concurrency 8. All 11,960 responses completed without client errors, NaNs, assertions, DMA timeouts, HBM fallback, or process death.

items.title: AMX software attention, canonical path: kernel + dispatch, default-off
items.body:
(This is #3879 trimmed and retitled: the third of the pieces the original PR was split into. The page-share counters (instrumentation that counts how many query tokens visit each KV page; default off) are #4267; a memory order fix is #4265; this updated PR, and the K mirror re-work is to be released. The history was rebuilt as four topical commits. The pre-split head 60d66d9c04 is kept as branch `jhan-amx-p0-pre-split`.)

## Short version

This PR adds an optional AMX path to software attention. The KV page must be a full 64-token page, and the query must be allowed to use every token of it. The model must have head size 128 (128 values per head) and 4 query heads per KV head. The model must also keep its queries in bf16. For such a page, the query-key scores and the softmax-weights-times-values product are computed with AMX tile multiplies. Every other page, model shape or number format runs the existing AVX-512 loop, unchanged. 

Both paths start from the same three lookups for a page: how many tokens it holds, whether the query may use it, and the positions of the query and of the page's first token. The AVX loop made these lookups already and applies its visibility and sliding-window rules token by token, as before. The lookups now run once, before the choice between the two paths. The AMX path adds whole-page tests on them: all 64 tokens in use, one visible range, first token inside the sliding window.

The build option TRON_AMX_DISPATCH is OFF by default, and a default build compiles no AMX feature. Setting the environment variable TRON_AMX_DISABLE=1 makes the AMX build run the AVX loop on every page. That build then produces the same output values as a build without the option.

## Words used here

- **AMX**: Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions, the tile-matrix instruction set of Sapphire Rapids and later Xeons. The measurement host is a Granite Rapids Xeon 6962P.
- **KV page**: 64 tokens of K and V. **kv_mul**: query heads per KV head (grouped-query attention); the kernels serve kv_mul 4 with head size 128, hence the namespace `amx_attn_h128g4` and the `_128x4` suffix.
- **dense page**: a page whose 64 tokens are all active, visible to the query in one range, and inside the query's sliding window. Only dense pages take the AMX path.

## What changed, by commit

1. **Kernels + interface + contract document** (`src/tron/kernels/amx_attn.cpp`, `h/tron/kernels/amx_attn_iface.hpp`): the query packer, the row-major QK kernel `qk_rowmajor_128x4` (K as stored is the A operand, packed Q the B operand, the result transposed on the way out: Note [QK orientation]) and `weights_times_v_128x4`; a typed `tron::bf16` interface; the kernel bodies live in one translation unit (one .cpp file compiled on its own; the build rule that gives it the AMX flags is commit 3); the runtime switch and its contract documented.
2. **Dispatch integration** (`h/tron/models/self_attention.hpp`, `h/tron/models/kv_cache.hpp`): `is_dense_amx_page` (the predicate), apply_dense_amx_page` (QK, the same scale/max/exp step as the dotter's epilogue (the step after its dot products), PV, the accumulator update, in one function; `apply_page_tok` calls it only after two checks, that a packed Q exists and that the page is dense) and `packed_amx_query` (at most one pack per token per call, done after the outer visibility and window checks and before the dense predicate); the raw V accessors `page::v_data` / `kv_block::v_base`. The dotter loop and its arithmetic are unchanged; the begin/end/position/visibility prologue it used moved above the dispatch so both paths share it.
3. **Build option + CI flag** (`CMakeLists.txt`, `src/tron/CMakeLists.txt`, `.github/workflows/cmake-single-platform.yml`, `README.ci.md`): `option(TRON_AMX_DISPATCH)` in the top-level `CMakeLists.txt`; when ON, `src/tron/CMakeLists.txt` adds the kernel source with the AMX compiler flags on that one file only. The CMake CI lane configures with the option ON, so the kernels and the dispatch compile whenever that lane's build step runs (a cached build artifact can skip it). The kernel cases of `t_amx_numerics` execute tile instructions only when the runtime check `available()` passes (an AMX CPU with OS tile support, in practice a Granite Rapids runner); elsewhere they print a warning and return. The workflow does not require a real-AMX execution for every candidate tip; that remains open (issue #3997).
4. **Tests** (`t/CMakeLists.txt`, `t/t_amx_numerics.cpp`, `t/t_amx_dispatch_dtype.cpp`, `t/t_llama_unit.cpp`, `config/test-benchmarks.json`): `t_amx_numerics` (the compile-time eligibility gate over the executors' activation scalars and the shape; packer layout compared bit for bit; QK against the AVX dotter within the fp32 add-order envelope; PV within the round-to-nearest versus truncation envelope), `t_amx_dispatch_dtype` (the production dispatch with CPU fakes, stand-in definitions of every kernel entry point that record their calls and run no AMX instruction: a bf16 executor packs once and calls QK and PV once for a full page; a 63-token page packs but calls neither kernel; float and fp16 executors never reach the fakes). `t/t_llama_unit.cpp` only swaps a literal 2 for the new named constant `KV_BLOCK_PLANES_2`; the eligibility case the original PR added there was dropped, because the first case of `t_amx_numerics` checks the same predicate.

Why these tests: the numerics test fails at compile time if the eligibility gate admits a float or fp16 activation scalar or a shape other than head 128 with 4 query heads per KV head, and at run time if the packer misplaces a value or if a kernel's result leaves the error envelope its inputs allow (fp32 add order for QK, the weight rounding mode for PV), which is the contract the dispatch relies on. The dispatch test fails if the type gate lets a float or fp16 executor reach the packer or if the dense predicate lets its 63-token page reach the kernels; it checks call counts and the captured query values, not attention outputs. The two tests protect different boundaries; both are cheap host tests, and the kernel cases need an AMX host.

## Review items from the first round

The seven inline comments Ben left on the canonical path have responses in the code and the document; a comment-by-comment map (old comment, new file and symbol, what changed) is the first comment below this description. Jeremy's two comments from Codex, the automated reviewer he ran (lazy setup; aligned pack buffer) keep the answers and measurements given on 2026-08-31; the pack buffer is `alignas(64)` storage of `tron::bf16` (the old head had aligned `uint16_t`).

## Evidence

All measurements were taken on delphi-3bda (Intel Xeon 6962P, a Granite Rapids CPU) with attention in software (USE_HW_ATTN=0). Words used: "clean" is a build made without the option; the "kill switch" is the AMX build run with TRON_AMX_DISABLE=1; an "arm" is one of these settings under comparison; a "placement" is the set of FPGA cards, CPU cores and NUMA node a run is pinned to.

There are two kinds of measurement. The runtron measurements compare two builds, the AMX build against a clean build, and their tokens/s are per user (each request's own rate in the runtron log). The nightly system tests compare one binary run twice, with and without the kill switch.

### runtron: qwen-3-4b tp2, 8 users, prompt 8192 tokens

**August measurement (2026-08-19).** Pre-split binaries, on cards 10:00.0 and 13:00.0 (socket 0). Decode was 14.50 tokens/s per user with the clean build and 17.04 with AMX, a gain of +17.5%. Prefill was 65.4 tokens/s per request clean and 124.5 with AMX, +90.5%.

**Repeat 1 (2026-09-07, shared machine, socket 1).** The same workload on commit 9723d56f62, whose code is this PR's. The machine was shared during this repeat, so the placement changed from August's: instance 2,4 on cards 90:00.0 and 93:00.0 (socket 1), with the application and device core numbers shifted by 72 and NUMA node 1 instead of 0. All three arms used this one placement. So the absolute tokens/s are not comparable with August's, but the AMX gain is: +17.7% here against +17.5% in August. The run was done twice; the two rounds agreed to 0.07 tokens/s (clean) and 0.001 tokens/s (AMX).

| Arm (Repeat 1, mean of two rounds) | Decode, tokens/s per user | Prefill time per 8192-token request (eight at once) | Prefill throughput per request, tokens/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| clean | 14.65 | about 122 s | 67.0 |
| kill switch | 14.75 (within 0.7% of clean; 0.8% and 0.5% in the two rounds) | about 122 s | 67.1 |
| AMX | 17.25 (+17.7%) | 53.6 s | 152.8 (+128%) |

The prefill gain, about +128%, is larger than August's +90.5%. These measurements do not separate the effect of the code change from the effects of the new placement and the shared host. Raw log: exec/results/qwen8u8k-pr1-half-20260907T1904.txt in the campaign repository.

**Repeat 2 (2026-09-07, free machine, August's placement).** Later the same day (21:15 to 21:31 UTC) the machine was free, and the same workload and commit were run again in August's placement: instance 0,4 on cards 10:00.0 and 13:00.0, socket 0, the same core lists as in August. Two rounds again.

| Arm (Repeat 2) | Decode round 1 | Decode round 2 | Decode mean | Prefill time per request | Prefill throughput per request |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| clean | 14.662 | 14.682 | 14.67 | 122.1 s | 67.1 tokens/s |
| kill switch | 14.795 | 14.764 | 14.78 (+0.7%) | 122.0 s | 67.2 tokens/s |
| AMX | 17.292 | 17.278 | 17.285, written 17.29 (+17.8%) | 53.6 s | 152.9 tokens/s (+128%, the same as on socket 1) |

Decode is tokens/s per user. With the placement equal to August's, the AMX decode gain (+17.8%) matches August's (+17.5%), and the absolute rates are within 1.5% of August's: 14.67 against 14.50 clean, 17.29 against 17.04 with AMX. Raw log: exec/results/qwen8u8k-pr1-20260907T1904.txt in the campaign repository.

### Nightly system tests, re-run 2026-09-04

One binary, run with and without the kill switch. These binaries were built before the rebase and before this split. 8 users, prompt about 1,024 tokens.

| Model and metric | Kill switch (AMX off) | AMX on | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| llama-3.1-8b tp2, decode tokens/s per user | 76.07 | 86.66 | +13.9% |
| qwen-3-4b tp4, decode tokens/s per user | 77.83 | 81.37 | +4.5% |

| qwen-3-4b tp4, MMLU Pro accuracy | 66.14% | 67.64% | +1.5 points, smaller than the 1.7 points between two unchanged runs of the AMX-off arm |


### Verification of this tip

Built and tested on 2026-09-07 on delphi-3bda (Intel Xeon 6962P, a Granite Rapids CPU).

The build used commit 9723d56f62 in a clean worktree. This PR's tip fcc7857 differs from that commit only in the cost-data file config/test-benchmarks.json, which no test reads.

CMake preset: cross-avx512, with -DBUILD_INGEST_MODELS=OFF (this only skips the ingest models). The tree was built twice: once with -DTRON_AMX_DISPATCH=ON and once with -DTRON_AMX_DISPATCH=OFF, the option's default. In both builds the three test targets and the tron library they link compiled.

Test results, as printed by Catch2 (the test framework):

| Test | Option ON | Option OFF (default build) |

| t_amx_numerics | All tests passed (4109 assertions in 4 test cases) | skip stub: All tests passed (1 assertion in 1 test case) |

| t_llama_unit | All tests passed (120054 assertions in 27 test cases) | All tests passed (120054 assertions in 27 test cases) |

With the option ON, t_amx_numerics printed no "AMX unavailable" warning. So its two kernel test cases ran real AMX tile instructions on this CPU.

The whole pre-split tree, rebased onto the same base commit, passed the same three tests with the option ON on 2026-09-06. That tree is the reference the split is checked against.

items.title: Value-initialize RX ring entries

labels.name: Skip benchmarks
labels.description: Skip benchmark jobs on the next pull request CI run

items.body:
## Summary

- Value-initialize `PosDevice::rx_entries` during construction.
- Remove the startup `memset` that overwrote live `rxinfo` objects.
- Remove the now-unused C string header.

## Why

`rxinfo` contains a `std::function<void()>`, making it a non-trivial type. Byte-zeroing the array after construction is therefore undefined behavior.

The ring does not require clearing after each use: `prepare_tail` and `rx_head` govern slot ownership, and producers overwrite the active request state before RX consumes a reused slot. Value
initialization preserves the intended initial zero/empty state without violating object lifetimes.

This does not change the ring protocol or public API. Completed entries remain available for diagnostics until their slots are reused.

## Validation

- `make format`
- `make lint`
- `make gen/t_worker_unit`

items.title: Preserve branch-local KV shard ownership

labels.name: Type: accuracy
labels.description: improves quality of results

items.body:
## Summary- 
move an indivisible partial shard onto the continuing child when prompt growth turns a leaf into an internal node- resolve shard lookup from the current edge so sibling branches cannot inherit a completed shard from the first branch- cover boundary relocation directly and exercise the production 128-token chunking path with a 1,715-token shared-prefix regression

## Root cause
When prompt growth exhausted a 1,600-token KV book, a partial [1024, 2048) shard could remain attached to an edge that had become internal. Later sibling prompts inherited that shard and its completed GOF DMA state, causing hardware attention to consume the first branch's KV data.

## Design alignment
This restores the ownership rules in doc/golden-gof-shard.md: only a leaf's final shard may be partial, a shard crossing a split moves whole to the continuing child, and sibling branches at the same token position own distinct shards. More specifically:
  - Partial shards belong only on terminal/leaf edges: doc/golden-gof-shard.md:26, doc/hw-kv-token-tree.md:342.
  - Spanning shards move whole to the child: doc/golden-gof-shard.md:34.
  - Same-position sibling shards must be distinct: doc/golden-gof-shard.md:25.

items.title: Remove redundant device index lookup
items.body:
## Summary

- remove the redundant `device_index_of()` scan from the HW-attention dump helpers
- use each `PosDevice`'s stored `idx` directly
- remove the now-unused global device-vector declaration and `<algorithm>` include

## Why

POS discovery assigns `PosDevice::idx` from the same dense index used to append the
device to the global `devices` vector, which is never reordered. Scanning that vector
again duplicates the existing invariant.

## Impact

Valid POS devices keep the same index. A pointer outside the global device vector no
longer produces a warning and a fallback index of zero; the dump helpers use the index
stored on that device instead.

## Validation

- `make format`
- `make lint`
- direct Clang syntax-only compile of `h/pos/hwattention_dump.hpp`
- cppix dependency index: 510 translation units, zero failures; the debug-only header

items.body:
## Summary

Add high-resolution FPGA state counters to Tron's existing Perfetto traces. Independent mailbox, attention, and weight samplers feed bounded queues, which separate hardware reads from Perfetto writes.

## Changes

- Enable host tracing with `--tracer-core`; opt into attention and weight MMIO reads with `--tracer-registers`. Select devices and sampler CPUs explicitly. Dice grants reject tracer CPU overrides in both runtron and Rinzler.
- Keep `--tracer-period-us` for FPGA mailbox updates and the host mailbox wait. Add independent `--tracer-register-period-us`: a 10 µs delay after each register pass by default, or `0` for unthrottled diagnostics. The achieved interval includes read latency and scheduling. Neither option changes the writer's 200 µs poll or minimum 1 ms utilization window.
- Decode mailbox, attention, and weight state into existing trace categories, with raw register halves and sampler diagnostics. All samplers use the writer's filtered device list and never read unsupported devices.
- Preserve independent device/category baselines, retry rejected emissions, and advance timestamps after partial rejection. Stop all samplers before device teardown.
- Add CI coverage and refresh affected Slice benchmarks.

`_rmem_bp` now inverts the active-high ready bit; account for this polarity change when comparing older traces. Unthrottled MMIO can perturb the workload. Sampling cannot guarantee every transition is captured.

## Test plan

- Format, lint, lint-notes, direct Nix lint-toolchain check, and full build: passed.
- Three sampler guard-page cases and three Rinzler flag cases failed before their fixes. The tracer binary now passes 34 cases and 1,276 assertions; all 110 wrapper tests pass.
- CI-equivalent Slice tests: 782 passed, 2 skipped. Refreshed `t_fpga_tracer` benchmarks at 1, 2, and 4 slices.
- Developer host gate (`--exclude-tag slow`): 86 passed, 0 skipped, 0 failed.

Earlier hardware validation at `edff02db`:

- Two FPGA suites each passed 48 tests and failed `t_mwaitx` at its timing bound (#1516). An isolated rerun passed; full-suite QA remains failed.
- Paired captures kept the mailbox near 100 µs while register cadence changed from 11.087 µs to 1.020 µs. Both inference requests completed without reported trace loss or sampler drops.
- All 53,502 decoded emissions matched. One of 260,166 held-value checks failed at the final weights group, consistent with documented partial emission at gate closure. The strict failure remains disclosed.

items.title: Add Perfetto memory allocator tracing

labels.name: Skip benchmarks
labels.description: Skip benchmark jobs on the next pull request CI run

items.body:
Add a debug-only Perfetto `memory` category for selective DMA and HBM allocator tracing without flooding steady-state allocation paths.

## Problem

Allocator pressure, HBM activity, heap expansion, reserve draining, large-slab acquisition, and OOMs were difficult to identify in existing Perfetto traces. Tracing every DMA allocation would produce excessive event volume.

## Solution

Register the debug-tagged `memory` category and add these selective allocator events:

- `hardware::allocator::allocate` — requested HBM allocation size
- `hardware::allocator::deallocate` — released HBM address
- `hardware::allocator::dump_profile` — profile tag; available with `HBM_ALLOC_SHADOW`
- `pos_heap_v2::expand` — number of DMA hugepages added
- `pos_heap_v2::drain_reserves` — number of cached slabs released
- `pos_heap_v2::oom` — requested size, size class, and caller addresses
- `slab_pool_t::acquire_large` — LARGE allocation size class
- `slab_pool_t::release_small_hugepage` — complete SMALL hugepage reclamation

Routine LARGE pre-drains and steady-state DMA allocation/deallocation remain untraced to avoid event flooding. Wildcard-only trace configurations do not enable this category; it must be explicitly enabled with `memory`. Structured trace assertions cover the event payloads, and the `t_hwalloc` Slice benchmark metadata is refreshed.

## Testing

- Default `build-test`, `t_heap_v2`, `t_hwalloc`, and `[perfetto]` passed; HBM-shadow `[perfetto]` and `[shadow]` passed
- `make lint`, `git diff --check`, and touched-file `clang-format-19 --dry-run -Werror`
- Dice `bin/slice bench --remote --remote-sku sku0 --update t_hwalloc` passed and refreshed the `genoa96` metadata
- DUT captures validated the expected memory events and annotations alongside model loading and generation activity

Each used llama-3.1-8b with hardware attention enabled (8K-token input, 64K-token output). Enabled traces contained 10,131 memory events; disabled traces contained none, and all traces had zero loss indicators.

items.title: Rebuild GOF page captures when a KV book relocates
items.body:
### Symptom

SIGSEGV after ~210 of 1204 MMLU-Pro questions. The signal handler catches SIGSEGV, logs a
backtrace, then aborts, so the core is recorded as SIGABRT.

Reproduced three times with a byte-identical stack (same binary file offsets each time), at 212,
207, and ~210 questions. Deterministic, not a flaky race.

### Stack

Resolved from the core with `addr2line -f -C -e gen/rinzler <offset>`:

| Frame | Offset | Symbol |
|-------|--------|--------|
| #5 | `0x20036ec` | `tron::hardware::gof::populate` — `src/tron/gof.cpp:155` |
| #6 | `0x1ea8712` | `std::__atomic_base<unsigned>::fetch_add` (shared_ptr refcount, inlined) |
| #7 | `0x2003dac` | `std::__shared_ptr<tron::hardware::shard>::get()` |

The caller frames put this on the **shard eviction/reacquire path**, which is exactly what
`populate`'s own comment predicts (`src/tron/gof.cpp:132-135`): it fires on first populate and
again after each eviction/reacquire.

### Root cause — confirmed by instrumentation

Proven on 2026-08-10 at HEAD `63e203c6c1f` with temporary diagnostics (`GOF_UAF`,
`RELOC_GALS`, `GOF_STALE_OFFSET`; all marked `TODO(crash-chase)`). The causal chain, with
matching book addresses from one run:

```
17:39:57.726  RELOC_GALS: edge at abs_ht 1471 repointing book 0x7f0d86e9d600
              -> 0x7f0da5002040 (shift 14) while holding 364 gals
              whose page captures are not updated
17:39:58.671  GOF_UAF: page_info[0] (token 1468) owner book 0x7f0d86e9d600
              freed before populate, layer 0
17:39:58.671  signal handled: Segmentation fault (11)
```

1. `defrag()` merges a child book into its parent and drops the last reference to the child
   (`full.hpp:1161` — "this defrag frees my_book").
2. `_relocate()` repoints the edge to the new book and invalidates the edge's append cache,
   but leaves `parent_edge.gals` holding page pointers into the **old** book.
3. The old book is freed.
4. The next `gof::populate()` on one of those gals invokes `k_head_fn`, dereferencing freed
   memory. SIGSEGV.

A gal's page_info captures a bare page pointer plus an offset into the book that owns the page. Defragmentation can splice that book into its parent and drop the old owner, leaving the capture dangling and causing gof::populate() to dereference freed memory.\n\nRebuild affected captures through the same factory used at construction. Walk the entire anchored subtree because a gal can straddle an edge boundary and reference an ancestor book from a descendant that owns a different book. Also document shard HBM ownership and release behavior.


<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **High Risk**
> Fixes a use-after-free in KV-book defrag and changes when wcls weight commands are posted to the device—both are correctness-critical paths that can crash or corrupt hardware state if wrong.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Fixes a deterministic UAF/SIGSEGV** when `defrag()` splices a child KV book into its parent: gal `page_info` captures kept bare `page*` pointers into the freed book, so later `gof::populate()` crashed.
> 
> After `_relocate`, the subtree now rebuilds affected captures via the same `make_page_info` factory used at construction. Repair walks the whole anchored subtree (not just edges still on the old book) because a gal can straddle an edge and reference an ancestor book from a descendant that owns a different book. Each `page_info` also records a weak `owner_book` so only captures for the moved book are rewritten.
> 
> **Separately**, wcls preparation now calls `defer_weight_commands_until_launch()` so its WCMD stays staged until `tx_launch` instead of posting during prepare while final-layer expert matmuls may still be active (which could corrupt the first W-Mem ping/pong block). Other matmuls keep prepare-time weight prefetch. Adds FPGA tests covering deferred staging and concurrent expert+wcls launch.
> 
> Also documents shard HBM ownership and release lifetime.
>

items.title: RX-stall, NaN, memory-bloat fixes
items.body:
## Summary

This PR fixes the RX-stall/NaN and memory-bloat issues that prevented us from reaching 
long-context / multi-user runs on GPT-OSS-120b. Also fixes independent HW-attention correctness, 
The combined changes allow four concurrent 128K contexts to complete prefill and decode without 
RXSTALL, command-ring corruption, metadata assertions, or hugepage OOM.

## Key changes

- Fix GOF dispatch across ancestor and sibling tree edges. A token save now credits every matching GAL target, and positional HW residency is derived from the contiguous completed-GOF prefix rather than a non-positional count.
- Defer GOF K/V staging allocation until DMA submission, avoiding long-lived staging buffers for inactive work while preserving the existing release/reacquire lifecycle.
- Keep prepared ACMD and metadata DMA sources valid for the full 512-request  preparation window. Metadata ownership now extends through RX completion, including correct device-aperture addressing across logical rollover. Included extending the ACMD buffer to 4096 in size, and the Metadata ring buffer to 65536.
- Preserve prepare-ahead WCMD MMIO performance without overflowing the 1,024-word hardware FIFO. Requests retain stable WCMD copies in `rxinfo`; prepare posts only within a 960-word window, launch publishes deferred commands in order, and RX returns word credits. A five-second launch timeout captures diagnostics instead of waiting forever if capacity stops advancing.
- Allocate raw HW result buffers before attention workers launch, closing a container-growth race.
- Enable model-selected HW attention by default and lower early launch to four-user aggregate batches.

## Validation

- `make format`, `make lint`, and `make build-test`
- Focused worker, GOF, scheduler, DMA tracker, and launch-threshold tests
- `t_gof_dma`: 4,871 assertions passed
- `t_hwattention_batch`: 227 assertions passed, including metadata rollover
- Four-user 128K run with prompt chunk limit 128: all four requests completed at 107.142 prefill tok/s/user and 22.165 decode tok/s/user (45.115 ms/tok), peaking at 340 KV books / 37.35 GB
- No RXSTALL, OOM, ACMD theft, or metadata assertion. The run observed one recoverable late `rxinfo overflow` and completed normally.

## Known FPGA constraints

- The AMEM query-group cap is a temporary host workaround until [llm_fpga#340](https://github.com/positron-ai/llm_fpga/issues/340) is fixed in deployed bitfiles.
- Compound HW-attention passes remain disabled because the current FPGA can strand the final one or two result words for those requests.


<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **High Risk**
> Changes core FPGA command lifecycle, GOF DMA residency, and HW attention scheduling on security- and correctness-critical inference paths; mistakes could corrupt rings, read uninitialized KV, or stall RX under load.
> 
> **Overview**
> Targets **long-context, multi-user GPT-OSS-style runs** that were hitting RX stalls, NaNs, ring corruption, and hugepage pressure.
> 
> **GOF / scheduler:** `gof_job` now holds **multiple targets** per query so K/V saves credit every matching GAL on ancestor/sibling edges; cooperative `gof_rodeo` carries `(job_ix, target_ix, layer)`. HW KV residency for shard push and attention planning uses **`count_complete_prefix_gofs()`** instead of a total count, so holes in out-of-order DMA cannot expose unread HBM. GOFs use **`deferred_staging`** so K/V buffers allocate at `prepare_for_dma()`; GAL creation is keyed by GOF-ending position with mates wired across split edges.
> 
> **POS worker / device:** Host **ACMD** and **metadata** shadow rings grow to cover the full 512-request prepare-ahead window; metadata ownership lasts until **RX** completion, with segmented DMA across device metadata aperture rollover. **WCMDs** are copied into `rxinfo`, published under `wcmd_post_mutex` with a **960-word** prepare window and word-level `wcmd_words_in_flight` credits returned on RX; launch posts deferred WCMDs in order. **Compound HW-attn split** is forced off; **`max_qs_for_emem`** gains a temporary **AMEM** cap (llm_fpga#340).
> 
> **Executor:** Raw HW result buffers are allocated during **plan assembly**; default **early HW launch** threshold drops to **4** users; model-selected HW attention default follows env unless `USE_HW_ATTN` overrides.
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit fa2798442b8cd00ea8376f2fb8b8f0e80bc93e3c. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup>

items.title: Add pass-windowed generation tracing to runtron
items.body:
## Summary

`--trace-passes SPEC` records only the named primary forward passes — trace
size is bounded by window width, not run length. `0` also captures startup
(init + model load).

    bin/runtron -m llama-3-8b -l 32 \
      --trace-gen story662.pftrace --trace-passes 0,5-8 -- "prompt"

Result: inference unchanged; the trace shows model load, a silent gap
(passes 1–4 gated), then exactly 4 `forward` slices with full detail, all
slices paired. Sample: `/scratch/bcraig/story662-traces/`.

## What

- New runtron option `--trace-passes SPEC` guiding Perfetto instrumentation
  (requires `--trace-gen` — a file path for in-process capture, or `traced`
  to record through the external daemon): application track events are
  captured only during the selected
  primary forward passes. SPEC is 1-based ranges (`2-4`, `500-`, `-150`,
  `10,60,100-110`); `0` selects **startup** — everything before the first
  forward pass (init, device bring-up, model load). Prompt parse is pass 1,
  not startup. Takes precedence over `--trace` when both are given.
- Emission-side gate: the TrackEvent macros in `h/common/perfetto.hpp` AND in
  a process-global atomic (storage isolated in `src/pos/trace_gate.cpp`,
  coupled to allocator tracing). The scheduler opens/closes the gate at the
  `full_scheduler::forward()` boundary via a per-scheduler pass counter
  (`h/common/trace_passes.hpp`); speculators/EAGLE children are excluded and
  no-work forwards do not count.
- Windowed runs use a duration-free in-process session — legacy `--trace` /
  `--trace-gen` keep their 5 s cap — with an exception-safe start/action/stop
  lifecycle on a core-0-pinned thread (`h/runtron/trace_lifecycle.hpp`).
  `--trace-passes` overrides `TRON_TRACE_FROM_TOKEN` (warns). Composes with
  `--trace-gen traced` daemon mode: the gate is emission-side and
  backend-agnostic.
- Response-slice pairing: the pre-forward "Generate response" BEGIN records
  iff the gate is open at that moment; the END restores the state captured at
  BEGIN, so the pair records or drops together — including repeated
  generations (`--isolated-iterations`), where the second run starts with the
  gate closed by the first run's teardown.
- Tests: `t_trace_passes` (unit — spec parser incl. the `0` grammar, pass
  counter, gate semantics, lifecycle, surrogate scheduler),
  `t_trace_passes_host` (integration on llama-3-8b-host — real forwards,
  in-process capture, pairing incl. the repeated-generation regression), CLI
  validation cases in `t_runtron_cli`; shared trace-inspection helpers in
  `t/trace_test_util.hpp`.

## Why

Legacy tracing is all-or-nothing: `--trace`/`--trace-gen` capture every pass
and stop at a hardwired 5 s, so long-run traces are either truncated or
unusably large, and there is no way to inspect a specific region deep in a
long generation. Pass windowing bounds capture by window width instead of run
length — measured on andoria-02: a 3-pass window of a 30-pass run is 927 KB
vs 9.1 MB legacy; an 11-pass window at pass ~7900 of an 8000-pass run is
6.5 MB. The `0` (startup) selector additionally captures init/model load,
which no legacy file mode records.

STORY-662 (Flow): https://www.notion.so/3a4d132d3cfd81599e7feb3fd9b98344

## Test plan

- `make test-host REMOTE=1` green via Distributed Dice (all host tests,
  including the three new binaries).
- The repeated-generation pairing fix (`eebdd5cad`) was verified red/green:
  with the fix stashed, the extended "keeps actual trace slices paired" case
  fails on the orphan response END; with the fix restored it passes. The
  regression test ships in this PR (`t/t_trace_passes_host.cpp`).
- Hardware validation on andoria-02 (llama-3-8b via Distributed Dice; all
  specs below with `--trace-gen FILE`). Analyzed with trace_processor SQL
  and a packet-level BEGIN/END walker:
  - `--trace-passes 2-4` (`-l 32`): exactly 3 `forward` slices, 0 unfinished;
    walker control: begins == ends exactly, response slice correctly absent.
  - `--trace-passes 0,5-8` (`-l 32`): 4 forwards; ~405 K loading-category
    events land before the first forward; passes 1–4 emit nothing (clean
    gated gap); response slice present and paired.
  - `--trace-passes 7900-7910` (`-l 8000 --dont-stop`): exactly 11 forwards,
    0 unfinished — the entire trace is the window, deep in an ~8000-pass run.
  - `--trace-passes 0,2-4 --isolated-iterations 2` (`-l 32`): pre-fix repro
    of the repeated-generation defect — walker measured the predicted orphan
    response END (ends = begins + 1); the `eebdd5cad` fix targets exactly
    this scenario.
  - `--trace-passes 5-` open-ended (`-l 32`): 28 complete forwards
    (passes 5 to end) plus one final forward truncated by session stop —
    the same stop-mid-slice signature the legacy baseline shows; a
    capture-boundary artifact of open-ended windows, not a pairing defect.
  - `--trace-passes 2-3` with both `--trace` and `--trace-gen` present:
    exactly 2 forwards — passes-windowed capture wins the precedence.
  - `--trace-passes 50-55` (`-l 128 --dont-stop`): exactly 6 forwards,
    0 unfinished.
  - `--trace-passes 120-` (`-l 128 --dont-stop`): 9 complete forwards
    (passes 120 to end) plus the same open-ended stop artifact.
  - `--trace-passes 10,60,100-110` (`-l 128 --dont-stop`): exactly
    13 forwards in three distinct clusters (disjoint multi-window works),
    0 unfinished.
  - Legacy `--trace-gen` baseline (`-l 32`): 30 forwards, whole run —
    9.1 MB vs 927 KB for the 3-pass window of the same workload.
- Sample capture for reviewers: `/scratch/bcraig/story662-traces/` holds the
  startup-spec trace (`0,5-8`) with a README of what to look for — drop it
  into ui.perfetto.dev or trace_processor to see the startup span, the gated
  gap, and the 4-pass window.
- `make format` and `make lint` clean at HEAD.
- Slice bench entries captured for the three new test binaries on `genoa32`
  and `granite_rapids_6962p` (one class per vendor); on the other two
  platform keys the tests use slice's unbenched fallback until someone
  backfills with a forced-class bench run.

## Risk & rollback

Tracing subsystem only; inference behavior is unchanged — the gate is
emission-side, defaults open, and legacy modes bypass windowing entirely
(pinned by a unit test; golden-logit tests untouched). Cleanly revertible: no
flags, migrations, or config to unwind.

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Touches global Perfetto macro overrides and scheduler tracing lifecycle; inference is emission-only with gate default-open, but Perfetto SDK bumps need macro re-validation.
> 
> **Overview**
> Adds **`--trace-passes SPEC`** (with **`--trace-gen`**) so Perfetto application track events are recorded only during chosen **primary forward passes** and optional **startup** (`0` = init/model load before pass 1). Pass specs use 1-based ranges (`2-4`, `500-`, `0,5-8`, etc.); windowed in-process traces drop the legacy **5s duration cap** and run until generation ends.
> 
> **Emission gating:** `h/common/perfetto.hpp` wraps TrackEvent macros with `application_track_events_enabled()`; the scheduler toggles the gate at `select_trace_pass()` / `complete_trace_pass()` around `full_scheduler::forward()` via `trace_pass_counter`. Speculators are excluded. **`stream_generate`** preserves BEGIN/END pairing for the "Generate response" slice across repeated generations.
> 
> **runtron** takes a dedicated windowed path (`runtron_trace_lifecycle`, `start_tracing(..., legacy_local_duration=false)`). **`--trace-passes`** wins over **`--trace`** and overrides **`TRON_TRACE_FROM_TOKEN`** (warns). Docs/`tronperf` help and tests (`t_trace_passes`, `t_trace_passes_host`, CLI cases) added; benchmark entries for new tests on two platforms.
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 1c41d959efe72d826818607908f0b60b21730216. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup>

items.title: boot-fvp: never pre-arm telnet in headless runs; tell the truth about the console
items.body:
An armed TelnetTerminal with no reading client back-pressures its UART after 16 KiB and the guest busy-spins on `UARTFR.TXFF` — a boot that "hangs" with the UART log frozen at exactly 16383 bytes, last line truncated mid-word. Headless runs with `ASIMOV_ENABLE_TELNET=1` (the combo DEVELOPMENT.md itself recommended for a live AP console) hit this a few seconds after the script exits at the boot marker; in bridge mode (userspace marker, past 16 KiB) such runs always timed out at 124 with the FVP left wedged. This is the "headless boot hang" from the Terminus+Asim thread.

The fix rides on a component fact: the telnet listener is bound regardless of `start_telnet`, so pre-arming a terminal in a headless run buys nothing — the console stays attachable either way — while costing the wedge.

## Changes

- **headless launches always pass `start_telnet=0` to the model** (`MODEL_TELNET`); `ASIMOV_ENABLE_TELNET=1 --headless` can no longer wedge a boot
- **`bp.terminal_0` is never pre-armed** (interactive included): the script only ever attaches a client to `ap_terminal`, and the BP UART carries no console output — an armed, undrained terminal there was the same trap waiting
- interactive mode unchanged in behavior: `ap_terminal` keeps `=1` and the script attaches its own client immediately
- the headless success message replaces the misleading "Telnet disabled. Re-run with ASIMOV_ENABLE_TELNET=1" (the port is open regardless) with the real contract: console log path, attach-anytime `telnet localhost <port>`, and the keep-reading caveat
- the timeout path hints at the one remaining stall cause — a client that attached earlier and disconnected/stopped draining — with the resolved port to reattach
- headless startup banner lists AP/BP/SCP UART logs explicitly (AP is the boot-marker + console log; it used to print only the output-less BP log). In passing, same class: the timeout `Check: tail -f` now points at the AP UART log, and the usage comment names `fvp-ap-uart-5.log`
- `DEVELOPMENT.md` knob row rewritten to match

## Verification (farm, this branch)

- trigger scenario A/B: `ASIMOV_ENABLE_TELNET=1 --headless` wedged at exactly 16383 bytes on the old script every time; with this fix it boots through to userspace (43K+ uart log)
- success path: boot to marker in 10.2s, new banner + Console/Attach messages print with the resolved port
- recovery claim: a deliberately wedged run was drained by attaching a reading client — log resumed 16383 → 43312 bytes, boot completed (what the hints promise)
- baseline: 45/45 headless boots (plain / BridgeFwd / BridgeFwd+asim) on the telnet-off path

## Remaining / out of scope

The attach-then-abandon stall is a one-way flow-control latch inside the ARM-binary component — nothing disables it in FM 11.30; the only safe states are "no client ever" or "a client that keeps reading". Mechanism write-up: terminus `model/DESIGN_LOG.md` § "TelnetTerminal: undrained console back-pressure"; launch-path hardening in the other repos: terminus#170, asimov-scp-firmware#95, asimov-tfa#39.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Script-only FVP launch and messaging changes; no auth, data, or kernel/runtime logic touched.
> 
> **Overview**
> Fixes headless FVP boots that could **hang after ~16 KiB of console output** when `ASIMOV_ENABLE_TELNET=1` pre-armed a telnet terminal with no draining client (TelnetTerminal UART back-pressure).
> 
> **`boot-fvp.sh`** introduces **`MODEL_TELNET`**: headless runs always pass **`start_telnet=0`** to **`ap_terminal`** (listener still attachable); interactive mode still pre-arms **`ap_terminal`** only. **`bp.terminal_0`** is always **`start_telnet=0`** (it is not the AP console and was the same trap). Headless success/timeout messaging now points at **`fvp-ap-uart-*.log`**, lists AP/BP/SCP UART paths, and documents attach-anytime telnet plus the keep-reading caveat instead of implying telnet is disabled.
> 
> **`DEVELOPMENT.md`** updates the **`ASIMOV_ENABLE_TELNET`** knob row to match that behavior.

items.title: Add host CPU temperature / frequency / power telemetry to Perfetto traces

labels.name: Continuous integration
labels.description: Relates to CI

items.body:
## Summary
Adds host CPU telemetry (temperature, frequency, package power) to Tron Perfetto traces,
complementing the sibling story's kernel/OS events. Closes #3198. Two independent layers
(they toggle separately):

- **App-side `hw` sampler** (`src/pos/hwperf.cpp`) — a background thread polls `/sys` and
  emits `TRACE_COUNTER`s on a new `hw` track_event category: hwmon CPU temperature,
  cpufreq avg/max, and RAPL `energy_uj` → Watts. Works in the in-process `--trace FILE`
  backend (unlike ftrace). On by default; `TRON_HW_SAMPLER=0` opts out,
  `TRON_HW_SAMPLER_INTERVAL_MS` tunes the 100 ms interval,
  `TRON_HW_SAMPLER_ALL_SENSORS=1` adds per-sensor temperature detail.
- **Hardware ftrace** — `power/cpu_idle` + `power/cpu_frequency` added to the `--os-events`
  overlay (daemon backend only).

### Tracks emitted, per socket

| Track | Source | Notes |
|-------|--------|-------|
| `socket<N> package temp (C)` | hwmon `Tdie`/`Tctl`/`Package id N` | one per socket |
| `socket<N> core temp min/avg/max (C)` | the per-die/per-core sensors | aggregated |
| `<driver> socket<N> <label> (C)` | every individual sensor | only with `TRON_HW_SAMPLER_ALL_SENSORS=1` |
| `cpu avg/max freq (MHz, N of M app cores)` | cpufreq sysfs | bounded sample, see below |
| `<domain> power (W)` | RAPL `energy_uj` | needs the grant below |

**Temperatures are aggregated by default.** The raw sensor count is large and
vendor-dependent — a dual EPYC exposes 26 (`k10temp`, 13/socket), a dual Granite Rapids
~146 (`coretemp`, one per core) — so the default is package + min/avg/max per socket (4
tracks/socket), which still surfaces a single hot die in the max. Per-sensor detail is one
env var away. Individual sensors are named `<driver> socket<N> <label>`, so a multi-socket
box never produces anonymous tracks.

**Frequency is a bounded sample, and the track name says how bounded.** A cold
`scaling_cur_freq` read blocks: reading all 384 cpus of a dual EPYC measures ~7.9 s per
pass on `acpi-cpufreq` (warm reads no cheaper), so a full scan can't run at trace cadence.
The sample is taken over the configured **app (compute) cores** — the cores tron actually
pins compute to — so a loaded run can't read as idle; it falls back to online cpus when no
app core list is configured. This needed one new accessor,
`tron::hardware::system::app_get_cpus()`, exposing the configured app cpu list (a snapshot
that `app_pin_thread()` doesn't consume).

## Why the diff touches runtron.cpp / perf.cpp (hw-sampler lifecycle)
The hw sampler's enable/disable is consolidated into the single
`start_tracing()`/`end_tracing()` pair (`src/pos/perf.cpp`) instead of being wired
separately into `runtron.cpp`'s phase callbacks + teardown and the SIGUSR1 path — so every
trace path (whole-run, phased `--trace-gen`, pass-gated `--trace-passes`, rinzler SIGUSR1)
enables the sampler at session start and disables it before the flush by construction. The
sampler thread starts once at `pos_startup()` and joins at `pos_shutdown()`; it parks on a
condition variable until a trace begins, so a process that never traces pays only a
sleeping thread (no periodic wakeups), and the first sample lands immediately on enable
rather than up to an interval later.

`disable_hw_sampling()` is a **real quiesce**, not a flag store: the sampler holds a mutex
across each tick body, so once `disable` acquires it no tick is emitting and none can
start. That is what lets `end_tracing()` flush a settled session. It costs at most one tick
body of blocking, on the trace-teardown path only.

⚠️ **One behavior change, now fixed.** An earlier revision of this PR moved
`disable_malloc_tracing()` in `runtron.cpp` such that the phased path no longer disabled it
after `join()` — so a phased run that ended before phase 3 left malloc tracing on for the
rest of the process and inflated `detected_mallocs()`. Caught in review; the post-join
disable is restored. Malloc tracing otherwise keeps its existing deliberate placement
(enabled after model load, so one-time load allocations stay out of the counter).

**Pre-existing hang, deliberately not fixed here:** on the phased path nothing counts
`tracing_end_latch` down when phase 3 never fires (`TRON_TRACE_FROM_TOKEN` above the tokens
actually produced, or an early stop), so `tracing_manager->join()` hangs. Only the *start*
latch has that fallback. Not introduced by this PR; tracked as STORY-689, and the comment
in `runtron.cpp` now says so instead of implying the case is covered.

## ⚠️ Security tradeoff — RAPL power loosens a CVE mitigation
`energy_uj` being root-only **is** the CVE-2020-8694 (PLATYPUS) power side-channel
mitigation. tron runs non-root, so `perfetto/grant-rapl-read` (invoked by `tronperf` /
`wrapper`) runs `sudo -n chmod a+r` on `…/intel-rapl:*/energy_uj`. **`a+r` re-exposes the
side channel to all local users until reboot.**

`a+r` is a deliberate choice rather than a mirror of the tracefs `chown -R $USER` alongside
it, and the asymmetry is the point: tracefs can afford exclusivity because ftrace is
single-owner anyway, so only one capture runs at a time regardless. RAPL is a read-only
counter with unlimited concurrent readers, wanted by plain `runtron --trace FILE` runs as
much as by daemon captures, and the grant outlives the run that made it (plain `runtron`
never calls the script — it inherits whatever state is there). `chown` would leave it
mode-400 owned by one user, so the next developer's capture silently strips power tracks
from a colleague's in-flight run. `README.perfetto.md` now documents this explicitly, with
`chgrp` to a shared group as the narrowing option for a multi-tenant host, and no longer
presents `chown` as the safe default.

Two hardening fixes from review: the grant is now a **no-op under `TRON_HW_SAMPLER=0`** (a
kernel-events-only capture never touches the mitigation), and it uses **`sudo -n`** so a
headless runner (`--detach`, LSF) warns and continues instead of appearing to succeed or
hanging on a prompt. When zones are present but unreadable the sampler logs that once,
naming the grant script, rather than dropping power silently.

## Testing
`t_hwperf` (host, `pos_fake`): **22 cases / 122 assertions**, all passing.

The layouts that decide whether counter names are correct and unique are covered against
**synthetic sysfs trees** (`TRON_HW_SAMPLER_SYSFS_ROOT`, and a root parameter on the
readers), because no single host exhibits them and several appear on no CI host at all:
sparse sensor indices, missing labels, non-sensor filenames, multi-socket ordinals, two
CPU-temp drivers loaded at once, package-label priority, RAPL name collisions, RAPL zones
present-but-unreadable, cpufreq bounding, and the app-core vs online-cpu selection. Plus a
sampler **lifecycle** case (park → enable → tick → disable → re-enable → teardown,
idempotent) and a **quiesce** case that sweeps `disable()` across the tick phase.

Three fixes were **mutation-tested** — the bug reintroduced, the suite confirmed red, the
fix restored:

| Reintroduced bug | Result |
|---|---|
| temp track named by device basename instead of driver + socket | 2 cases fail |
| `disable_hw_sampling()` as a bare flag store (no quiesce barrier) | fails 3/3 runs |
| frequency sample strided over all cpus instead of app cores | 2 assertions fail |

The quiesce case needed the phase sweep to have teeth: written the obvious way — wait for a
tick, then disable — it passes even with the barrier removed, because `disable` then always
lands in the interval sleep.

### Still outstanding (needs real hardware — not run)
- **`config/test-benchmarks.json` entries recorded for 2 of the 4 platform keys**:
  `granite_rapids_6962p` (delphi-3af6, 1.76/1.65/1.65 s, 10 MB) and `genoa32`
  (andoria-11, 1.34/1.36/1.35 s, 9 MB). `genoa96` and `granite_rapids_6960p` are still
  unbenched for `t_hwperf`, because the hosts that report those keys are currently
  unusable — andoria-cf8c fails its Dice health check (EACCES on
  `/opt/positron/bin/dice`, reported separately) and delphi-17bb is `closed_Adm`.
  Partial coverage is the norm for this file: 32-49 other tests are missing per key.
- ~~Re-validate the capture rows on both vendors.~~ **Done** — see "Capture validation" below.
- **Unresolved Intel claim:** that `coretemp` caches each sensor's MSR read for ~1 s. Attempted
  from a 20 ms Intel capture: 41 samples over a 1.1 s window, 1 value change — which cannot
  separate 1 Hz caching from coretemp's 1 °C quantisation. The in-process backend can't settle
  it (see the 5 s window note below); needs a daemon capture. Impact is cosmetic — 8 tracks
  either way, and repeated counter samples render as a flat line.

## Usage
```
# whole-run, in-process file backend (hw counters, no daemon):
gen/runtron --trace out.trace -m <model> ...
# full app + kernel + hw timeline (daemon backend):
perfetto/tronperf --os-events --output-file out.trace -m <model> ...
# rinzler serving (SIGUSR1 timed capture):
perfetto/wrapper --os-events -n rinzler -c rinzler
# per-die temperature detail:
TRON_HW_SAMPLER_ALL_SENSORS=1 gen/runtron --trace out.trace -m <model> ...
```
Disable the sampler with `TRON_HW_SAMPLER=0`.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

## Capture validation (2026-07-31, both vendors)

Three in-process captures through `bin/runtron --remote` (exclusive whole-box leases), analysed
with PerfettoSQL. Both vendors pass every structural check.

**Intel — delphi-3af6 (Xeon 6962P):** 8 aggregate temp tracks exactly (`avg` fractional over 72
cores, min/max integral at 1 °C); **146** per-sensor tracks under `TRON_HW_SAMPLER_ALL_SENSORS=1`
(73/socket, all `coretemp socket<N> <label>`), with the aggregates still present so detail is
additive; **0** per-sensor leakage in the default run; **0** PCI-named tracks;
`cpu avg/max freq (MHz, 8 of 112 app cores)` — "app cores", and 112 matches the app cpu list
counted independently from runtron's log; RAPL `package-0`, `package-1`,
`dram (intel-rapl:0:0)`, `dram (intel-rapl:1:0)` with the `dram` collision qualified, 187–297 W
per package and **0** negative samples; 14 tracks / 14 unique names; sampler cadence mean
**107.9 ms** against the 100 ms interval.

**AMD — andoria-11 (`genoa32`):** **18** per-sensor tracks = 9/socket (`Tctl` + `Tccd1..Tccd8`;
that box has 8 CCDs per socket), named `k10temp socket0 Tccd1 (C)` etc. — **this is the item-4
validation**, since AMD is the only vendor with two same-driver hwmon instances and the old code
emitted `0000:00:18.3 Tccd1 (C)` here. **0** PCI-named tracks; 8 aggregates; 28 tracks / 28
unique; `8 of 55 app cores` cross-checked. Aggregation math verified **exactly** against the raw
sensors: `core temp min` series min = 40.875 = min over all `Tccd*`, `core temp max` = 54.125 =
max over them, and every `package temp` value appears in the `Tctl` series.

**RAPL power was absent on andoria-11 — and correctly explained.** That host's `energy_uj` is
root-only (unlike andoria-02 and delphi-3af6, which sit at `444`) and the in-process `--trace`
path never invokes the grant script, so the sampler logged once:
`hw telemetry: 0 of 4 RAPL energy zones readable; package power will be omitted from the trace
until access is granted (perfetto/grant-rapl-read, …)`. That is review item 9 validated in
exactly the scenario it was written for; previously the power tracks disappeared silently.

### Note for anyone repeating this: the in-process trace window is ~5 s, not the run

`perfetto_duration_ms = 5 * 1000` (`src/pos/perf.cpp:28`) and `--trace FILE` passes
`legacy_local_duration = true`, so the session stops 5 s after `start_tracing()` regardless of
run length; the hw series is shorter still (~2.4 s at 100 ms) because the sampler thread starts
at `pos_startup()` partway in. This also explains the `Flush() called, but tracing has not been
started` pair at exit — expected on any run over 5 s, not a sampler symptom. Pre-existing; long
hw series need the daemon backend.

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Touches tracing teardown (quiesce before flush), a detached sampler thread with sysfs I/O on core 0, and optional widening of RAPL sysfs permissions (`a+r`) on shared hosts; runtron malloc-tracing cleanup was adjusted to avoid leaving tracing enabled after phased runs.
> 
> **Overview**
> Adds **host hardware telemetry** to Perfetto via a new `hw` track category: a background sysfs sampler (`hwperf.cpp`) emits temperature, bounded cpufreq, and RAPL-derived power as `TRACE_COUNTER`s while tracing is active. This works in **in-process `--trace FILE`** captures as well as daemon traces; `--os-events` separately adds `power/cpu_idle` and `power/cpu_frequency` ftrace.
> 
> **Sampler behavior:** polls hwmon (aggregated per-socket temps by default), strided cpufreq over configured **app cores** (`app_get_cpus()`), and package power when `energy_uj` is readable. Lifecycle is tied to `start_tracing()` / `end_tracing()` with a quiescing disable before flush; the thread is spawned at `pos_startup()` and torn down at `pos_shutdown()`. Env knobs: `TRON_HW_SAMPLER`, interval, optional per-sensor temps, test sysfs root.
> 
> **RAPL access:** `perfetto/grant-rapl-read` (called from `tronperf`/`wrapper`) uses `sudo -n chmod a+r` on RAPL energy counters when needed; docs spell out the CVE-2020-8694 tradeoff and group-scoped alternatives. Grant is skipped when the sampler is off.
> 
> **Other:** extensive `t_hwperf` coverage (synthetic sysfs + lifecycle), benchmark entries for two platforms, README/skill updates for querying `(C)`/`(W)`/`(MHz)` tracks. `runtron.cpp` restores post-join `disable_malloc_tracing()` on whole-run traces.
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 5a9dc830f74fee566c86185f20a80d58895de53f. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup>

items.title: WLR Hw-Attention Stage 3

labels.name: Performance
labels.description: Makes things go faster

items.body:
## Summary

Stage 3 of hardware attention: extends the HW path from single-query decode to
**multi-query prompt parsing**, fenced by EMEM/metadata capacity, together with the
GOF DMA-transfer plumbing and ingest codegen that drive it. The development history
is consolidated into four reviewable blocks.

## High-level blocks

**1. GOF DMA transfer tracking & lock-contention refactor**
`shard.hpp`, `gof.*`, `dma_tracker.cpp`, `hwattention.hpp`, `driver.cpp`, `device.hpp`
Contiguous per-layer started/done DMA prefixes with out-of-order hole handling,
reservation rollback, watermark accounting, and SW-only-layer premarking so the done
prefix flows over layers that never DMA. Batches K/V block submission through a single
critical section (`xfer_n_blocks`) to cut lock contention, plus the supporting
`DmaQueue` descriptor plumbing.

**2. Multi-Q HW prompt parsing, EMEM-fenced**
`self_attention.hpp`, `model.hpp`, `worker.cpp`, `hw_attn_config.*`, `common.hpp`, scheduler
HW attention for prompt prefill with batched Qs (up to `MAX_B`) and multiple physical
subpasses when KV spans more shards than EMEM allows. `construct_hw_plan` builds
EMEM-safe passes and coalesces compatible prompt queries; the worker shares one K/V
load per batch and emits per-Q metadata per subpass; the scheduler stops blanket
HW→SW folding for multi-query edges and reconciles short queries / causal tails above
the HBM boundary. HW attention gated off for non-ingested models.

**3. Ingest codegen + C++ entry points**
`ingest/src/*.hs`, `model.hpp`
Emits `{Launch,Prepare}{Prompt,NonPrompt}HwAttention` statements from the ingest
pipeline so ingested models drive HW attention during prompt parsing, plus the C++
entry points they target (early-launch batch-size gate and prepare/launch forwarders).

**4. cursor[bot] review findings**
Hardens the metadata-ring batch budget (`MAX_HW_SUBPASSES_PER_PASS` + a `static_assert`
on ring capacity), gates `use_hw_attn_for_this_model` on EMEM capacity so models whose
head count exceeds EMEM fall back to SW consistently (with a correct disable-reason
log), fixes the `WARN_IF_METADATA_WRAPS` block so it compiles, removes leftover
commented-out debug scaffolding, and re-enables the golden generate tests that were
hidden behind dotted Catch2 tags.

🤖 Summary generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

---

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
> [!NOTE]
> **High Risk**
> Touches correctness-critical HW attention, metadata ring ownership, GOF DMA concurrency, and scheduler HW/SW partitioning; wrong gating or completion ordering can silently corrupt attention output.
> 
> **Overview**
> **Multi-query hardware attention for prompt prefill** replaces the single-Q-only path: `construct_hw_plan` coalesces compatible prompt queries, splits passes by EMEM shard limits and up to `MAX_HW_SUBPASSES_PER_PASS` physical subcommands, and carries per-query causal boundaries (`last_hw_token_pos`). The POS worker batches up to `MAX_B` Qs with shared K/V loads, per-Q metadata per subpass, `activ2proc` capped by `max_qs_for_emem`, and joins multiple subpass results on unpack. HW completion uses a per-layer generation counter instead of a bool to avoid RX races.
> 
> **GOF / KV DMA plumbing** moves per-layer DMA state into a side-table with reservations (`try_reserve_gof_dma`), contiguous started/done prefixes with out-of-order holes, and SW-only layer premarking. GOF K/V upload uses `prep_xfer` + `xfer_n_blocks` under one queue lock. `dma_tracker` completion calls `mark_gof_dma_done` on the shard API.
> 
> **Enablement and scheduler** add `use_hw_attn_for_this_model()` (EMEM `max_shards_for_emem` gate, `USE_HW_ATTN` with per-model default via `force_hw_attn`), `maximum_hwattn_batch_size`, bitfile-gated HW-attention WLR, and `MIN_TOK_IDX_FOR_HWATTN` 127. The scheduler keeps multi-query HW plan entries and reconciles short queries and causal tails above the HBM boundary instead of folding all multi-Q edges to SW.
> 
> **Ingest** emits batch-size-gated early/late `maybe_*_hw_attention` around `save_k`/`save_v` and sets `force_hw_attn` on ingested models. New FPGA batch test `t_hwattention_batch` and EMEM gating unit tests accompany the change.
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 5b7c076a9e6a09f7aee25d72722af10483255736. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup>

items.title: busybox: enable taskset for core pinning
items.body:
Enables the busybox `taskset` applet in the Asimov rootfs.

**Problem:** The rootfs shipped without `taskset`, so there was no way to pin a process to a specific CPU core.

**Solution:** Turn on `CONFIG_TASKSET` in the board busybox config, plus `FEATURE_TASKSET_FANCY` + `FEATURE_TASKSET_CPULIST` so the `-c` cpu-list form works (`taskset -c 3 ./app`). `-c` depends on FANCY in busybox kconfig, so all three are needed; this matches busybox upstream defaults.

**Testing:** Built busybox from this config and ran it natively — applet present in `--list`, `--help` shows the `-c LIST` form, `/usr/bin/taskset` lands in busybox.links, and `taskset -c 0 … -c -p` pins to core 0 and reads the affinity list back.

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Config-only change that adds a standard BusyBox utility; no auth, data, or runtime logic is modified.
> 
> **Overview**
> The Asimov rootfs **busybox** build config now ships the **`taskset`** applet so processes can be pinned to specific CPU cores on the device.
> 
> **`CONFIG_TASKSET`**, **`CONFIG_FEATURE_TASKSET_FANCY`**, and **`CONFIG_FEATURE_TASKSET_CPULIST`** are turned on in `br2-external/board/asimov/busybox.config`, enabling the **`-c` cpu-list** form (e.g. `taskset -c 3 ./app`). FANCY is required for `-c` in BusyBox kconfig; this matches typical upstream defaults.
> 
> No other files change—**`asimov_defconfig`** already points at this busybox config, so the next image build picks up **`/usr/bin/taskset`** via the usual busybox symlinks.
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 19d87a9f4a4ed962fd1fd140c933b726d28bd669. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup>

items.title: Add temporary benchmark-only PR workflow

labels.name: Continuous integration
labels.description: Relates to CI

items.body:
## Summary

- Add a temporary benchmark-only pull request workflow.
- Gate it by the `dev-benchmark-only` label and PR author allowlist.
- Reuse the existing PR benchmark matrix and benchmark report comment path.

## Notes

- Allowlisted PR authors: `mcherba`, `Wado-posi`.
- The workflow has no dependency on lint, build, or test jobs.
- The workflow must exist on `main` before `pull_request` `labeled` events can trigger it.
- Intended as a temporary workflow for the current AoF development push.

## Validation

- `make format`
- `make lint`
- `bin/ci/lint-ci-pins.sh`
- YAML parse check


<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> CI-only addition reusing existing benchmark scripts; gated by label and two allowlisted authors on self-hosted runners.
> 
> **Overview**
> Adds **`.github/workflows/benchmark-only-pr.yml`**, a temporary GitHub Actions path that runs PR benchmarks **without** the main lint/build/test CI graph.
> 
> **Triggers:** `pull_request` on `labeled`, `synchronize`, and `reopened`. Jobs run only when the PR has the **`dev-benchmark-only`** label, the author is **`mcherba`** or **`Wado-posi`**, and (for `labeled` events) the label added is that one—not other labels.
> 
> **`benchmark` job:** Same self-hosted matrix as existing PR benchmarks (`2x96core` / `2x72core`), including cache check, `uv` sync for torch export when needed, FUSE mount, **`bin/ci/ci-run-benchmark.sh`**, and cleanup.
> 
> **`benchmark-report` job:** After benchmark success or failure, generates the unified report via **`bin/ci/generate_benchmark_report.sh`** and posts or updates the standard “### Benchmark of” PR comment.
> 
> Workflow comments state it should be removed after the current development push.
>
